conventions.convention: Domination uses a supplied sigma-finite positive measure on the experiment's fixed measurable sample space. It adds no parameter sigma-algebra or parameter measurability.
The likelihood ratio of P1 against P0 is dP1,ac/dP0, defined under AC as a P0-almost-everywhere class. It represents the full law P1 only when P1 is absolutely continuous with respect to P0.

Under AC, likelihood densities are simultaneously selected finite-valued nonnegative measurable representatives. Likelihood fixes the observation and varies the parameter labels; no parameter measurability, canonical pointwise version, or common exceptional null set for an arbitrary uncountable parameter set is asserted.

Change of measure requires P1 absolutely continuous with respect to P0 and applies to nonnegative measurable functions, including extended integrals, and to real-valued P1-integrable measurable functions.

Equivalent dominators give a positive common density factor almost everywhere. Ratio equality is asserted separately for each fixed parameter pair where denominators are positive; no value is assigned at zero denominators.

The nonnegative RN representative lemma assumes AC and sigma-finiteness of both positive measures and supplies a finite-valued representative on the original measurable space, without assuming completeness.

load_bearing.statement: Assume AC. If μ and ν are sigma-finite positive measures on the same measurable space and ν ≪ μ, then the Radon–Nikodym class dν/dμ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative μ-almost everywhere.

For an experiment dominated by a fixed sigma-finite positive measure μ, under AC select simultaneously finite-valued measurable nonnegative representatives pθ of dPθ/dμ. For fixed observed x, Lx(θ) = pθ(x) is the likelihood; no parameter measurability or common exceptional null set for arbitrary uncountable Θ is implied.

Assume AC. For probability measures P0 and P1 on the same measurable space, decompose P1 = P1,ac + P1,s relative to P0 and define the likelihood-ratio density of P1 against P0 as the P0-almost-everywhere class dP1,ac/dP0. It is a full density of P1 only when P1 ≪ P0.

Assume AC and let P0,P1 be probability measures on one measurable space. Let r be a nonnegative measurable representative of the likelihood-ratio class for P1 versus P0. If P1 ≪ P0, then E_P0[g r] = E_P1[g] for every nonnegative measurable g, and also for every real-valued P1-integrable measurable g. Without P1 ≪ P0, this identity need not hold because the singular component may be nonzero.
Let ν be a finite positive measure and μ a positive measure on the same measurable space. If ν = νac + νs with νac ≪ μ and νs ⊥ μ, then νac and νs are positive measures.
A statistical experiment is dominated by a supplied positive measure μ on its measurable sample space when μ is sigma-finite and Pθ ≪ μ for every θ.

alerts.finding: The Statement starts 'Let ... be standard Borel' and the Given lists the spaces, statistic, model, reference law and absolute continuity, but neither includes AC. Its Facts explicitly say '[A1] ... the Radon–Nikodym theorem is used under AC', and proof steps 1.1 and 3.1 invoke that assumption. The proof's declared choice assumption should also appear in the Statement and Given; the cited batch-4 change-of-measure theorem explicitly assumes AC.

The Statement says 'Let f,g:X→[0,+∞] be measurable. Then' followed by the density-substitution identity involving μ. Its Given likewise mentions only the functions. Neither binds μ or the ambient sigma-algebra. The cited def-measure-with-density requires a measure space (X,A,μ). State that ambient measure-space hypothesis explicitly; the displayed proof otherwise supplies the standard valid argument.

The Statement says 'Let f,g:X→[0,+∞] be measurable and let c≥0' and then asserts integral inequalities involving μ. The Given again omits μ and the ambient sigma-algebra. The simple-minorant argument is sound on an arbitrary measure space, but that setting is not explicitly bound in the proposition.

seams_checked.note: The experiment definition and prerequisite page supply a fixed measurable sample space and parameter-indexed probability laws without parameter measurability. The domination definition preserves that interface and adds only the supplied sigma-finite dominator.

Checked the discrete ratio definition, countable-mixture theorem, exponential-family definition, common-reference criterion and standard-Borel factorization criterion. Density and change-of-measure uses retain the required domination, ratio direction and parameter-specific null sets. The common-reference criterion's omitted Statement-level AC assumption is separately alerted.

The score definition, score identity and scalar Cramér–Rao theorem use selected finite nonnegative RN densities. Differentiability, common support and derivative envelopes are supplied as additional hypotheses rather than inferred from domination.

The ratio-measurability lemma, randomized test definition, exact-size lemma and Neyman–Pearson proof use finite nonnegative common-dominator densities. They keep {p0=0<p1} separate and do not infer P1 ≪ P0 from common domination. The α=0 and α=1 branches are addressed.

This is contextual rather than a direct likelihood citation: all four A-page items use measurable membership or acceptance events and require neither domination nor parameter measurability. The page makes no stronger likelihood claim and explicitly includes auxiliary randomization when inverting randomized tests.

Directional KL, finite-hypothesis mutual information, Pinsker and Fano use dP/dQ only under P ≪ Q. Non-AC KL is assigned +∞; nonnegative change of measure is applied to separate logarithm parts before signed integration. The finite mixture dominates each hypothesis.

The DQM definition uses one supplied sigma-finite common dominator and nonnegative density versions with explicit AC convention. It claims version invariance only through individual L2 norms, without requiring a common exceptional null set. The score theorem uses density normalization and adds no parameter-measurability claim.
